lessons.title: Reading: The Last Sermon of Rasoolullah (SAW)
lessons.notes_html:
The Last Sermon

Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him) is the last Rasool (Messenger) of Allah. He is Khatam-un-Nabiyyin — the final Prophet, after whom there is no prophet. He delivered his Last Sermon (Khutbah) on the 9th of Dhul Hijjah, 10 years after Hijrat, in the Uranah valley of Mount Arafat, during his last Hajj. Its message was directed to all humanity.

Main Teachings of the Sermon

  • The blood (life), property and honour of every Muslim are sacred — as sacred as the day of Arafat, the month of Dhul Hijjah and the city of Makkah. No one may harm another Muslim's life, property or honour.
  • Blood revenge of the Days of Ignorance was abolished. The first claim of blood revenge abolished was that of Ibn Rabi'ah bin Harith. No one may take revenge for a murder on his own; justice is through law.
  • Riba (usury) — the extra amount (interest) charged on a loan — was declared forbidden. All claims of interest were remitted (cancelled), beginning with the interest due to Hazrat Abbas bin Abdul-Muttalib.
  • People were advised to worship Allah, offer the five prayers, fast in Ramadan, pay Zakat willingly and perform Hajj. Zakat is an act of worship and obedience to Allah.
  • The path of righteousness means living according to the commands of Allah, doing good deeds, avoiding sins and injustice, and holding fast to the Quran and the Sunnah.

Equality of Mankind

The sermon declares: "All mankind is from Adam and Eve. An Arab has no superiority over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab. A white has no superiority over a black, nor a black over a white, except by piety and good actions." In the sight of Allah, the only standard of superiority is piety and good actions (taqwa). Every Muslim is a brother to every Muslim, and the Muslims constitute one brotherhood.

Importance and the Last Point

The Last Sermon is a complete message and code of life: protection of life, property and honour, rights of women, equality of mankind, worship of Allah, and following the Quran and Sunnah. Rasoolullah (peace be upon him) left behind two things to follow: the Book of Allah (the Holy Quran) and his Sunnah. The last point of the sermon was 'Bearing Witness': he asked, "Have I not delivered the Message of my Lord?" The people replied, "Yes, you have." He then said three times, "O Allah! Bear witness," and asked those present to convey the Message to those who were absent.

Key Points

  • The Last Sermon was delivered on 9th Dhul Hijjah, 10 AH, at Arafat.
  • Life, property and honour of every Muslim are sacred.
  • Blood revenge and usury were abolished forever.
  • Superiority is only by piety and good actions — all human beings are equal.
  • The Quran and the Sunnah are the guidance left behind for us.

lessons.title: Speaking and Study Skills: Rhetorical Questions and Silent Letters
lessons.notes_html:
Rhetorical Questions

A rhetorical question does not expect a real answer; it makes the listener think and reinforces the speaker's point. A real (ordinary) question expects an answer.

  • Not rhetorical (real questions): "Do you know where my pencil case is?" "What time do you get home from school?" "How many students are there in class today?"
  • Rhetorical: "If we don't stop this now, when will it ever end?" "What is wrong with society today?" "Who does she think she is?" "Is it fair that millions of people are starving all over the world?" "Is it not clear that I would like to win this race?"

Making Rhetorical Questions

  • "They are taking a very long time to get here." → "How long do we have to wait for them?"
  • "We need to end animal cruelty before it's too late." → "How can we keep watching animals suffer in silence?"
  • "We should promote healthy eating in school." → "Don't our children deserve healthy food at school?"
  • "Everyone wants to be famous." → "Who doesn't want to be famous?"
  • "We have only one earth to take care of." → "If we do not take care of this earth, who will?"
  • Useful stems: "Does not everyone believe that ____?" "____, can they?" "Is it not time to ____?" "How can we continue to let unhealthy ____?"

Silent Letters

A silent letter is written in a word but not pronounced. From the unit's words:

  • right — 'gh' silent; righteousness — 'gh' silent
  • whom — 'w' silent; whether — 'h' silent
  • listen — 't' silent; could — 'l' silent
  • comb — 'b' silent; honour — 'h' silent; hour — 'h' silent
  • knowledge — 'k' silent; people — the final 'e' is silent
  • reckon — there is no silent letter; 'ck' together gives the /k/ sound.

Key Points

  • A rhetorical question makes a point; it does not ask for an answer.
  • Questions asking for facts (time, number, place) are real questions, not rhetorical.
  • Silent letters are written but not pronounced, e.g. 'k' in knowledge and 'b' in comb.

lessons.title: Vocabulary: Prefixes and Suffixes
lessons.notes_html:
Word Meanings (Glossary)

  • sermon: an address on a religious or moral subject.
  • sacred: very important; greatly respected.
  • entrust: to make someone responsible for taking care of someone or something.
  • blood revenge: taking revenge for a murder.
  • deliberately: with a definite intention.
  • waive: refrain from insisting on or using (a right or claim).
  • committed: pledged or bound to a certain course or policy; dedicated.
  • chastise: to punish. mission: goal; objective.
  • superiority: the quality of being superior. deliver: to bring and hand over.
  • righteousness: the quality of being morally right or justifiable.

More Dictionary Meanings

  • concise: brief, clear and to the point. reckon: to think, suppose or consider.
  • usury: lending money at a very high rate of interest (riba). obligation: a duty or commitment.
  • inflict: to cause something unpleasant or painful to be suffered. earnest: serious and sincere in intention.
  • apostle: a messenger; one sent on a mission. sacred trust: a holy responsibility that must be guarded faithfully.

Prefixes and Suffixes

A prefix is a group of letters put before a root word which changes its meaning. A suffix is a group of letters put at the end of a root word. Examples from the unit: unhurt = not hurt; pre-war = before the war; tireless = never feeling tired; the root word in 'unemployed' is 'employ'; 'un-' added to 'finished' gives 'unfinished' (work still to be done); '-ed' is a suffix; 'cook' + '-ing' = cooking; 'peace' + '-ful' = peaceful.

Labelling Words

  • helper: help (root) + er (suffix). kindness: kind + ness. careful: care + ful.
  • unchaste: un (prefix) + chaste. inequity: in + equity. non-Arab: non + Arab.
  • righteousness: right + eous + ness. undeniable: un + deny + able.
  • commitment: commit + ment. unsuccessful: un + success + ful. directed: direct + ed.

Key Points

  • Prefix comes before the root word; suffix comes after it.
  • un- often means 'not'; pre- means 'before'; -less means 'without'.
  • The root word carries the main meaning of the word.

lessons.title: Grammar: Pronoun–Antecedent Agreement
lessons.notes_html:
The Rule

A pronoun must agree with its antecedent (the noun it stands for) in number and gender. A singular antecedent takes a singular pronoun; a plural antecedent takes a plural pronoun.

The Book's Sentences Solved

  • I bought a book. It proved very useful. (book — singular)
  • We see with our eyes. (agrees with 'we')
  • The farmers were working with their hands. (farmers — plural)
  • We saw animals in the zoo. They looked beautiful. (animals — plural)
  • The boy who whistles is my brother. He whistles loudly. (the boy — masculine singular)
  • The students missed six questions. They were challenging. (the questions — plural)
  • One of the birds flapped its wings. (one bird — singular)
  • The new style of dress is popular; I like it. (style — singular)

Using a Dictionary

The unit also teaches us to look up words in a dictionary and note their syllable division and part of speech: appreciate — ap-pre-ci-ate (verb); humanity — hu-man-i-ty (noun, uncountable); sacred — sa-cred (adjective); piety — pi-e-ty (noun, uncountable); forbidden — for-bid-den (adjective); astray — a-stray (adverb); inequity — in-eq-ui-ty (noun, uncountable). Guide words at the top of the dictionary page, the entry word, its pronunciation, definition, syllable division and part-of-speech abbreviation help us fill such a table.

Key Points

  • Choose the pronoun that matches its antecedent in number and gender.
  • 'One of the...' takes a singular pronoun (its), because it points to one.
  • Countable/uncountable applies to nouns, not to verbs or adjectives.

lessons.title: Writing: Topic Sentences and Summary Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Topic Sentences

The topic sentence carries the main idea of a paragraph. The topic sentences of the first four paragraphs of the unit are:

  • Introduction: "Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him) delivered his last sermon (Khutbah) on the ninth of Dhul Hijjah, 10 years after Hijrat, in the Uranah valley of Mount Arafat."
  • Life and Property: "Your blood, your property and your honour are as sacred as this day, this month and this city."
  • Blood Revenge and Usury: "Behold! All practices of paganism and ignorance are now under my feet; the blood revenge of the Days of Ignorance is remitted."
  • Rights of Women: "O people! Fear Allah concerning women; verily you have taken them on the security of Allah."

Writing a Summary

A summary gives only the key ideas of a text, in your own words. An objective summary includes no personal opinion. The unit's summary of the Last Sermon: delivered at Arafat on 9th Dhul Hijjah 10 AH, the sermon is a complete code of life for all humanity. It declares life, property and honour sacred, abolishes blood revenge and usury, protects the rights of women, commands prayer, fasting, Zakat and Hajj, teaches that all human beings are equal and superior only by piety, and leaves the Quran and the Sunnah as guidance. At the end, the people bore witness that he had delivered Allah's Message.

Key Points

  • The topic sentence tells the main idea of the whole paragraph.
  • A summary keeps key ideas only and drops examples and details.
  • An objective summary has no personal opinion of the writer.
  • Write the summary in your own words, not by copying the text.

lessons.title: Reading: Martyrs of Pakistan
lessons.notes_html:
Who Are the Martyrs?

The martyrs (Shuhada) of Pakistan are the brave soldiers and citizens who sacrificed their lives for the defence and honour of Pakistan. A martyr is a person who gives his life for a noble cause, especially for his country and faith. 'Major' is a military rank — the rank of a senior officer in the army, above Captain and below Lieutenant Colonel.

Major Tufail Muhammad Shaheed

  • He was commissioned in the 16th Punjab Regiment in 1943 and commanded many appointments.
  • In August 1958, Indian troops had captured a village called Lakshmipur in East Pakistan. As a company commander in East Pakistan Rifles, he was given the task of freeing the village.
  • He divided his men into three groups and attacked during the dark hours of 7th August 1958, encircling the illegal Indian post.
  • About fifteen yards from the enemy line, his group came under heavy fire. He silenced the enemy's machine gun with a grenade and, although fatally wounded, crawled towards the enemy commander and kept directing the operation until the enemy was driven out.
  • Four enemy troops were killed and three were taken prisoners. He was awarded the Nishan-e-Haider for his valour.

Rashid Minhas Shaheed

  • Rashid Minhas was a Pilot Officer in the Pakistan Air Force, commissioned in 1971 and posted to PAF Base Masroor, Karachi; he was a pilot under training.
  • His instructor, Matiur Rahman, wanted to seize control of the aircraft to hijack it and take it to India.
  • Rashid Minhas is the only PAF officer to receive the Nishan-e-Haider, and the youngest and shortest-serving recipient — he was only 20 years old.
  • He was laid to rest on 21st August 1971 with full military honours and was posthumously awarded the Nishan-e-Haider.

Military Honours

Military honours are awards and medals given by the state for bravery, gallantry and distinguished services. The Nishan-e-Haider is the highest military award in Pakistan; others include Hilal-e-Jurat, Sitara-e-Jurat and Tamgha-e-Jurat. They are awarded to officers and soldiers of the armed forces who show extraordinary courage — very often posthumously to martyrs. Captain Muhammad Sarwar Shaheed was the first martyr awarded the Nishan-e-Haider (1948, Kashmir). We pay homage to our martyrs on Defence Day, 6th September, by remembering their sacrifices, visiting memorials, praying for them and honouring their families.

Oral Communication

In the book's dialogue, a school counsellor advises a student: apply to more than one good school; research each school's strengths and weaknesses on the Internet and read brochures; make the application strong by being authentic and honest, listing accomplishments, awards and special talents without exaggeration; and prepare for an interview with punctuality, neat formal dress and confidence.

Key Points

  • Nishan-e-Haider is Pakistan's highest military award, given for extraordinary bravery.
  • Major Tufail Muhammad freed Lakshmipur in August 1958 and was martyred leading his men.
  • Rashid Minhas, the youngest Nishan-e-Haider recipient, stopped his aircraft from being hijacked to India.
  • Defence Day is celebrated on 6th September.

lessons.title: Reading: Literary and Functional Texts
lessons.notes_html:
Two Kinds of Texts

Texts are broadly of two kinds. Literary texts are written for pleasure, imagination and art — poems, novels, short stories, drama and fables. Functional texts are written for practical purposes — memos, notes, brochures, instructions and notices; they are non-fiction.

  • A poem is the text that contains a rhyme scheme, rhythm or meter.
  • Aesop's Fables is a literary text — short animal stories with morals.
  • Science fiction is also a literary text; it is imaginative writing about science and the future.
  • Fantasy belongs to the genre of fiction.
  • Functional texts such as memos, notes and brochures are non-fiction.

Key Points

  • Literary texts aim at imagination and enjoyment; functional texts aim at practical use.
  • Rhyme scheme, rhythm and meter are features of a poem.
  • Genre means the kind or category of a text, e.g. fiction, poetry, drama.

Word Meanings (Glossary)

  • battalion: a large group of soldiers. assign: to give someone a particular job.
  • evict: to force someone to leave. martyrdom: death of a martyr.
  • commission: the position of an officer in the army. valour: great courage.
  • cockpit: an area in a plane where the pilot sits. absconding: leaving hurriedly or secretly.
  • wrest: forcibly pull something from a person's grasp. deliberately: on purpose; intentionally.
  • posthumously: happening after someone's death. reverence: great respect and admiration.

More Dictionary Meanings

  • distinguish: to recognise or treat as different; to make oneself known for excellence.
  • troop: a group of soldiers. illegal: not allowed by law; unlawful.
  • violate: to break or disobey a law, rule or boundary. grenade: a small bomb thrown by hand.

Correct Spellings (-able / -ible Words)

lessons.title: Grammar: Verbs — Helping Verbs and the Simple Past Tense
lessons.notes_html:
Helping Verbs and Main Verbs

The main verb expresses the main action. Helping verbs — forms of be, do, have and modals like can, may, will, would — are used with main verbs to tell when an action takes place and to make negatives and questions.

  • She is writing a novel. (helping: is → main: writing)
  • I have bought a villa. They have gone by bus. (have → bought / gone)
  • They may not resist it. I will answer the call. Would you stay at home?
  • He did not read it. We were basking in the sun. You are reading my mail.

The Simple Past Tense

The simple past tense is used for actions and events that happened in the past. For regular verbs we add '-ed' to the root form; irregular verbs have their own past forms (spend → spent, fight → fought). Past-tense verbs in the unit: crossed, spent, divided, missed, embraced, graduated, seized, created, fought.

Making Negatives in the Past Tense

Use did not + first form of the verb: He won a medal → He did not win a medal. I made notes → I did not make notes. They worked in fields → They did not work in fields. You ate cereal → You did not eat cereal.

Filling Blanks with the Simple Past

  • Many years ago, it was (be) very difficult to live without electricity.
  • They finished (finish) their homework. The troops came (come) under heavy fire.
  • My sister wrote (write) lots of postcards. We went (go) fishing last Saturday.
  • At the age of 17, he joined (join) Pakistan Air Force Academy. I got (get) up late last Sunday.

Key Points

  • Helping verbs support the main verb; they include is, are, was, were, have, has, did, will, would, may.
  • After 'did not', always use the first form of the verb.
  • Learn the irregular past forms: be→was, come→came, write→wrote, go→went, get→got, spend→spent, fight→fought.

lessons.notes_html:
The Writing Process

The book's writing process has these steps: pre-writing, research, drafting, revising, editing and proofreading. First collect ideas and facts, then draft the paragraphs, then revise, edit and proofread them before the final copy.

Model Paragraphs (from the book)

Nishan-e-Haider is the highest military award of Pakistan. The word 'Haider' is one of the titles of Hazrat Ali (RA), the lion of Allah, and the award is named after his bravery. It is given only for the most extraordinary acts of courage in the face of the enemy, and every recipient so far has embraced martyrdom in earning it.

The first Nishan-e-Haider was awarded to Captain Muhammad Sarwar Shaheed in 1948. Since then, heroes like Major Tufail Muhammad, Major Raja Aziz Bhatti, Rashid Minhas and Captain Karnal Sher Khan have received it. Rashid Minhas is the only Air Force officer and the youngest recipient of this honour.

The significance of Nishan-e-Haider is very great. It reminds us that our freedom and safety rest on the sacrifices of our martyrs. It teaches the young generation the values of courage, loyalty and love for the motherland, and it keeps the memory of our heroes alive forever.

Key Points

  • Begin with a clear opening paragraph that introduces the topic.
  • Give facts in the middle paragraphs: the first recipient, famous recipients, and what makes the award special.
  • End with the significance — the lesson the topic teaches us.
  • Always revise, edit and proofread before finalising your writing.

lessons.title: Reading: The Poem 'A Nation's Strength'
lessons.notes_html:
The Poem's Question

In the first stanza the poet wonders what makes a nation's pillars high and its foundations strong, and what makes it mighty enough to defy (resist) the enemies that crowd around it. 'Pillars' and 'foundations' are metaphors: the nation is compared to a building. Its pillars are its great, strong men — the leaders and heroes who support it — and its foundations are the basic principles, values and common people on which it stands.

What the Poem Rejects

  • Gold: "Not gold but only men can make / A people great and strong." Kingdoms built on gold fell in battle because their foundations rested on sinking sand, not on abiding rock.
  • The sword: empires that trusted in the sword also passed away and their glory decayed.
  • Pride: worldly power and pride are worthless in the sight of God. Pride, the 'bright crown' which nations loved, was struck down by God — "God has struck its luster down in ashes at his feet."

The Poem's Answer

The brave men who make a nation strong work while others sleep and dare while others flee. They stand fast for truth and honour and are ready to suffer long for their nation. With these qualities they build the nation's pillars deep and lift them to the sky. The qualities that make a people great — truthfulness, honour, bravery, hard work, daring and readiness to suffer — belong to character, not to health or wealth.

Structure of the Poem

The whole poem is built as question and answer. The first stanza asks what makes a nation strong; the middle stanzas reject gold, the sword and pride one by one; the last stanzas answer positively by picturing the brave men. So the poem moves from question and rejection to a clear, hopeful conclusion. The second last stanza says in simple words: money cannot build a great nation; only truthful, honourable and patient men can.

Central Idea

The central idea of the poem is that the real strength of a nation lies in the character of its people, not in its wealth, weapons or pride. Only brave, truthful and self-sacrificing men can make a people great and strong.

Oral Communication

A tag question is added at the end of a statement to invite the listener to agree and keep the conversation going, e.g. Shiza says, "It is a hot day, isn't it?"

Key Points

  • Men, not gold, make a nation great and strong.
  • Pillars = great men; foundations = principles and people (metaphors).
  • Kingdoms on gold stand on sinking sand; nations on character stand on abiding rock.
  • The poem's pattern is question → rejection of false answers → true answer.

Word Meanings (Glossary)

lessons.title: Grammar: Apostrophes and Types of Sentences
lessons.notes_html:
The Apostrophe

An apostrophe shows possession (belonging) or the omission of letters in contractions.

  • It's in the main building of my college. (It is — omission)
  • Othello is a character in Shakespeare's play. (possession, one owner)
  • They are buying babies' clothes. The boys' chairs are yellow. (plural owners — apostrophe after s)
  • The guard's cap is on the sofa. The principal's office. The cat's milk. Ahmad's books.
  • I don't think that my father's shirt will fit me. We're going to our friends' house. (contractions)

Types of Sentences

  • Declarative sentences state an idea and end with a full stop: "The house is near the post office." "They were not in a hurry."
  • Interrogative sentences ask for information and end with a question mark: "Would you hand me the ruler?" "Do you know their address?"
  • Imperative sentences give commands, instructions or polite requests: "Write your name at the top of the page." "Please open the window." "Look both ways before you cross the street."
  • Exclamatory sentences express strong emotion and end with an exclamation mark: "How beautiful this flower is!" "What a beautiful scene it is!"

Key Points

  • For a singular owner, add 's; for plural owners ending in s, add only an apostrophe.
  • Don't confuse 'its' (belonging to it) with 'it's' (it is).
  • Judge the type of a sentence by its job and its end mark.

lessons.title: Writing: Writing an Argument
lessons.notes_html:
What Is an Argument?

An argument supports a claim with evidence and ends with a conclusion. The book's task: write an argument to support the claim that only "Strong People make a Nation Strong".

The Model Argument

  • Claim: Only strong people make a nation strong.
  • Evidence: History shows that rich and powerful empires fell when their people became weak, proud and lazy, while poor nations rose when their people were brave, honest and hardworking. Pakistan was defended in 1965 and in every war by the courage of its soldiers and the unity of its people, not by gold. Emerson's poem also says that brave men who work while others sleep and dare while others flee build a nation's pillars.
  • Conclusion: Therefore, it is the strength of character of its people that makes a nation truly strong, and we should build our character to make Pakistan strong.

Key Points

  • State your claim clearly in the opening lines.
  • Support the claim with evidence: facts, examples from history and the text.
  • Finish with a conclusion that restates the claim in the light of the evidence.

lessons.title: Reading: Review of Units 1–3
lessons.notes_html:
Main Points of the Last Sermon

  • The life, property and honour of every person are sacred.
  • Blood revenge of the days of ignorance is abolished.
  • Usury (riba/interest) is forbidden and all interest claims are cancelled.
  • Women must be treated kindly and their rights respected.
  • Worship Allah: offer five prayers, fast in Ramadan, pay Zakat and perform Hajj.
  • All mankind is equal; superiority is only by piety and good actions.
  • Hold fast to the Quran and the Sunnah.
  • Those present must convey the message to those absent.

The Sermon protects human life and property so that society lives in peace; it ends the old customs of revenge and interest which caused feuds and exploitation; it raises the status of women; it removes all pride of race, colour and family by declaring equality; and it leaves the Quran and Sunnah as the permanent guide. It is a complete charter of human rights and duties.

Homage to the Martyrs

Major Tufail Muhammad Shaheed attacked the illegal Indian post at Lakshmipur in the dark hours of 7th August 1958, silenced the enemy machine gun with a grenade, and kept directing his men though fatally wounded, until the enemy was driven out. We pay homage to such heroes by remembering them on Defence Day and Youm-e-Shuhada, praying for their souls, visiting their graves and memorials, honouring and helping their families, naming schools and roads after them, and teaching their stories to children.

Values and the Poem's Message

A nation increases its national pride through bravery, honesty, truthfulness, hard work, unity, discipline, justice, equality and love for the homeland. The general message of 'A Nation's Strength' is that the real strength of a nation is the character of its people; gold, military power and pride cannot make a nation lastingly great.

Rhyming Words

Rhyming pairs from the poem: rust — must; grand — sand; brown — down; flash — ash; pride — bride; high — sigh; strong — throng; might — flight; empire — aspire; suffer — rougher.

Oral Communication

Statements can be turned into rhetorical questions: "You should visit the Lahore Fort" → "Who wouldn't want to visit the Lahore Fort?" "Everybody wants to go to Jinnah Garden" → "Who doesn't want to go to Jinnah Garden?" "You can recycle tins, plastic and glass" → "Can't we all recycle tins, plastic and glass?"

Key Points

  • The Last Sermon is a complete charter of human rights and duties.
  • Homage means honouring the martyrs in word and action, not only in ceremonies.
  • National pride rests on the character and values of the people.

lessons.notes_html:
Rights of a Member of Society

Every member of a society enjoys certain rights: the right to live safely, to get education and health facilities, to speak and worship freely, and to be treated equally and justly. These rights are protected by the law and by the teachings of our religion; the Last Sermon itself declared life, property and honour sacred.

Duties of a Member of Society

Along with rights, we also have duties. We must obey the law, pay our taxes, keep our surroundings clean, respect the rights and property of others, help the poor and needy, and take part in the welfare of our community. A good citizen never harms others and always puts the interest of society above selfish gain.

The Balance of Rights and Duties

Rights and duties go together. If every member of society performs his duties honestly, everyone can enjoy his rights in peace, and the nation becomes strong and prosperous.

Key Points

  • Write one paragraph on rights and another on duties to keep the essay balanced.
  • Connect your ideas with the units: the Last Sermon's teachings support these rights.
  • End with a conclusion that joins rights and duties together.

lessons.title: Reading: Quaid-e-Azam
lessons.notes_html:
Why 'Quaid-e-Azam'?

Muhammad Ali Jinnah is called 'Quaid-e-Azam' (the Great Leader) because of his far-sightedness and leadership qualities. His life was full of struggle, sacrifice and untiring efforts, and under his leadership the Muslims of India got a separate homeland — Pakistan. His leadership qualities were: far-sightedness, honesty, principle, devotion and untiring hard work; he united the Muslims on one platform through country-wide tours; he was a brilliant lawyer and a wise strategist who planned every step carefully.

From Unity to the Two-Nation Theory

  • In the early days of his politics, Jinnah was the proponent (great supporter) of Hindu-Muslim unity and played an important part in the Lucknow Pact (1916) between the Congress and the Muslim League.
  • The Two-Nation Theory means that the Hindus and Muslims of India were two separate nations: they belonged to two different religious philosophies, social customs, traditions and civilizations, and could not live together as one nation. Jinnah said it was a dream that Hindus and Muslims could ever evolve a common nationality.
  • 'Resolve their differences' means to settle disagreements and end internal quarrels. The Quaid asked Muslims to do this so that they could unite on one platform with a common bond with the Muslim League — only a united nation could win freedom.

Key Events

  • The Nehru Report was rejected by all shades of Muslim opinion because it spoiled the efforts of Hindu-Muslim unity and ignored Muslim demands — it did not accept their separate electorate and safeguards. In reaction, the Quaid presented his famous Fourteen Points.
  • In the elections of 1937, the Muslim League won some 108 out of 485 Muslim seats. The results proved the League was the only all-India party for Muslims. Congress formed governments in seven of eleven provinces and treated the Muslims brutally.
  • The demand for Pakistan (1940) shattered forever the Hindus' dream of a Hindu empire on the British exit, started an era of Islamic renaissance and creativity, and made the creation of Pakistan inevitable.
  • The British exit was an era of Islamic Renaissance because the Muslims awoke from inertia, discovered they could live as a separate nation, and a new spirit of revival, unity and creativity arose among them.
  • In the Round Table Conferences (London, 1930–32), the Quaid played a vital role in the federal structure sub-committee and presented the Muslim demands with great legal skill.

Oral Communication

In the book's dialogue, Tariq and Shaukat talk about summer vacations: Shaukat visited his native village, enjoyed swimming in the pond, and learnt to ride and climb trees from his cousins. Natural expressions used include 'That's great', 'That's cool' and 'I am glad you had an amazing time.'

Key Points

  • Lucknow Pact 1916 — Jinnah, the ambassador of Hindu-Muslim unity.
  • Nehru Report rejected → Fourteen Points presented.
  • 1937 elections: Muslim League won 108 of 485 Muslim seats.
  • Demand for Pakistan (1940) made Pakistan inevitable.

lessons.title: Grammar: Articles, Adjectives and Adjectival Phrases
lessons.notes_html:
Articles: a, an, the

'The' marks a noun as definite. 'A' is used before a noun beginning with a non-vowel (consonant) sound, and 'an' before a noun beginning with a vowel sound.

  • We live in the same street. ('same' takes 'the')
  • I like to eat an apple a day. I have got an idea. (vowel sounds)
  • The Spanish language is related to Latin. The Muslim League represented the Muslims.
  • Quaid-e-Azam was a man of principle. He had a great love for nature.
  • We must put corruption down with an iron hand. Jinnah played an important role. His brother is an engineer. (iron, important, engineer begin with vowel sounds)

Adjectives: Attributive and Predicative

Adjectives used before a noun are attributive; adjectives used after the noun or verb are predicative.

  • Attributive: a nice trip; a different civilization; separate electorates; my eldest daughter; country-wide tours.
  • Predicative: Children were happy. They were hungry and tired. My parents were glad. She came first. The children were asleep.

Making Adjectives from Nouns and Verbs

Adjectives are formed by adding suffixes like -able, -ful, -less, -ous, -ish, -ive, -ant, -ent: help → helpful; child → childish; pain → painful; fool → foolish; attract → attractive; resist → resistant; oil → oily; hope → hopeful; danger → dangerous; differ → different; dust → dusty; success → successful.

Adjectival Phrases

An adjectival phrase does the same job as an adjective and describes a noun: 'at the bookstore' (describes 'the man'); 'in the cage' (the lion); 'long and spotted' (the snake); 'for Pakistan' (the demand); 'in the blue jacket' (the man); 'extremely delighted' (Everyone). Model uses: "The wet road was very slippery after the rain." "She came out of the examination hall beaming with joy." "The annoyingly loud music kept us awake all night."

Key Points

  • Choose a/an by the sound of the next word, not its spelling.
  • Attributive = before the noun; predicative = after the verb.
  • An adjectival phrase describes a noun, just like a single adjective.

Dictation Words of the Unit

Learn the spellings of these words for dictation: sacrifice, separate, resolution, philosophy, literary, electorate, aspiration, sentiments, tremendous, committee, renaissance, shattered. Practise by reading, covering, writing and checking each word.

Using a Mind Map

The book gives a mind map for the essay on Quaid-e-Azam: man of his word; a man of principle; leadership qualities; devotion to his cause; an intelligent student; devoted hard worker; a great lawyer; strategical management. A mind map collects the main points before writing, so the essay stays organised.

Model Essay (from the book)

Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah was the founder of Pakistan and one of the greatest leaders of the world. As a student he was intelligent and hardworking, and he became a great lawyer through his devotion and ability. He was a man of principle and a man of his word: whatever he said, he did, and he never compromised on the rights of the Muslims. His leadership qualities were matchless. He organised the scattered Muslims on one platform, planned his strategy wisely, and led the Pakistan Movement with complete devotion to his cause. He worked untiringly, day and night, even when his health was failing. Because of his far-sightedness, honesty and strategical management, the dream of Pakistan came true on 14th August 1947. Truly, he deserves the title of Quaid-e-Azam — the Great Leader.

Key Points

  • Plan the essay with a mind map before you start writing.
  • Give each quality of the Quaid a place in the essay with a supporting fact.
  • End with a strong concluding line that sums up the whole essay.

lessons.title: Reading: Smog
lessons.notes_html:
What the Picture Shows

The unit opens with a picture of a city road covered with thick smog, in which buildings and vehicles can hardly be seen. It makes us think about the serious problem of air pollution in our cities, especially in winter.

The Ozone Layer and the Teacher's List

The ozone layer is a layer of ozone gas high up in the atmosphere which protects the earth and living beings from the harmful ultraviolet rays of the sun. Besides smog, the teacher enumerated seven environmental issues facing the world: deforestation, overpopulation, water pollution, climate change, global warming, ozone layer depletion and air pollution.

Causes of Smog

Smog is mainly a product of burning a large amount of high-sulphur coal and the vapours and smoke emitting from automobiles. In Lahore it is caused by a combination of vehicle and industrial emissions, smoke from brick kilns, the burning of crop residue, general waste and dust from construction sites, along with large-scale cutting of trees.

Lahore and the Air Quality Index

  • Lahore has been called one of the most polluted cities in the world. Once termed the city of gardens, its Air Quality Index (AQI) once reached about 550, whereas air is safe to breathe only if the quality is up to 50.
  • Every winter, the cities in the upper and central parts of Pakistan wear a blanket of fog; surface pollutants thicken the fog into smog.

Effects of Smog on Health

Invisible particles penetrate every cell and organ of our bodies, causing acute and chronic diseases including asthma, strokes, heart attacks and dementia. They also increase the risk of respiratory diseases and lung cancer, and poor air quality badly affects mental health too.

Protecting Ourselves and the Atmosphere

  • The teacher's safety tips: use a face mask; remove contact lenses and use regular glasses; drink extra water; blow your nose regularly; wash hands and face when you come indoors; avoid going out unnecessarily; seal vents and windows; use air purifiers; drive carefully and slowly in smog and use fog lights.
  • Measures being taken: checking and fining smoke-emitting vehicles, shifting brick kilns to cleaner zigzag technology, action against burning crop residue, tree-plantation drives, AQI monitoring, and closing schools and offices on very hazardous days.
  • We can keep the atmosphere clean by planting trees, reducing vehicle and factory smoke, not burning residue and waste, using public transport and clean fuels, and keeping vehicles properly tuned.

Oral Communication

In the book's dialogue, Anjum is stressed out because of school, his job, housework and sports. Mumtaz advises him: "You really ought to take a vacation" and go to a hill station for a week. Anjum at last agrees to think about it seriously.

Key Points

  • Smog = smoke + fog, thickened by pollutants.
  • Safe AQI is up to 50; Lahore once reached about 550.
  • Smog harms lungs, heart, brain and mental health.

lessons.title: Vocabulary: Word Meanings and Homophones
lessons.notes_html:
Word Meanings (Glossary)

  • smog: a form of air pollution that looks like a mixture of smoke and fog, especially in cities.
  • deforestation: the act of cutting down or burning trees in an area.
  • dementia: a brain condition, mostly affecting older people, causing difficulties with memory, thinking and control of the body.
  • hazardous: involving risk or danger, especially to health or safety.
  • residue: a small amount of something that remains at the end of a process.
  • industrialisation: the process of developing industries in a country or area.
  • particle: a minute portion of matter. issue: a problem or worry.
  • fog: a thick cloud of very small drops of water in the air close to the land or sea, difficult to see through.
  • sulphur: a chemical element.

More Dictionary Meanings

  • depletion: the reduction or using up of something (ozone layer depletion = thinning of the ozone layer).
  • emit: to send out or give off (smoke, gas, light). pollutants: substances that make air, water or soil dirty and harmful.
  • intensify: to become or make stronger and more serious. sustained: continuing for a long time; steady.
  • standstill: a complete stop. acute: severe and sudden (of disease). chronic: lasting for a long time (of disease).

Homophones

A homophone is a word that is pronounced like another word but is different in meaning or spelling.

  • our / hour: Our business is growing rapidly. / You are one hour late.
  • low / law: The sun is low in the sky. / We must obey the law of the country.
  • sight / site: At first sight, the city looked beautiful. / This is the site for our new school building.

  • check / cheque: Please check your answers. / He paid the fee by cheque.

Key Points

  • Homophones sound the same but differ in spelling and meaning — choose by sense.

lessons.title: Grammar: Personal Pronouns and Apostrophes
lessons.notes_html:
Personal Pronouns

A personal pronoun is a word used in place of a person's name — I, we, you, he, she, they, it, me, us, them. Choose the pronoun that matches the noun it replaces:

  • Mahd and Fahd → They are brothers. Your sister → Is she at school?
  • Nazar, Mazhar and Kazim → They work in the bank. The pigeon → It is on the roof.
  • The cat and the dog → They are my pets. The door → It is locked.
  • My brother and I → We live together. Qamar, Saba and I → We are friends.
  • Qasim → He is going to Japan. Elephant → It is the biggest land animal. Saliha → She went to school.

Apostrophe for Plurals of Letters and Numerals

Use an apostrophe and 's' to form the plurals of letters, numerals and signs: The word has two a's. Dot all the i's and cross all the t's. How many b's are in 'bamboo'? (Two — b-a-m-b-o-o. The solved book prints 'One', which is a misprint.) There are three 5's in that number.

Apostrophe for Possession

  • the light of the moon → the moon's light. six years time → six years' time.
  • the surface of the earth → the earth's surface. Somebody's cap is on the desk. the house of the people → the people's house.
  • My neighbour's cat is black and white.

Apostrophes in Contractions

Don't (do not), You've (you have), They'll (they will), I'd (I would), It's (it is/it has), Let's (let us), didn't (did not), o'clock (of the clock); dropped figures in dates: the summer of '98, the '60s.

Key Points

  • 'It' is used for animals and things; 'we' is used when the speaker is included.
  • The apostrophe has three jobs here: possession, omission, and plurals of letters/figures.

lessons.title: Writing: An Essay on the Causes of Pollution and Its Solutions
lessons.notes_html:
The Model Essay

Introduction: Pollution means the dirtying of our air, water and land, and it has become one of the biggest problems of the world.

Causes: Its main causes are smoke from vehicles and factories, burning of coal, crop residue and waste, cutting of trees, overpopulation, and the throwing of garbage and chemicals into rivers. In our cities, these causes produce smog, which damages our lungs, eyes, heart and mind.

Solutions: The solutions are in our hands. We should plant more trees, keep our vehicles tuned, use public transport, stop burning waste and residue, shift factories and brick kilns to clean technology, and keep our streets and rivers clean. The government should enforce the laws strictly, and every citizen should play his part.

Conclusion: If we act together today, we can give our children a clean and healthy Pakistan tomorrow.

Key Points

  • Organise a problem essay as: introduction — causes — solutions — conclusion.
  • Match every solution to a cause (burning residue → stop burning; smoke → clean technology).
  • End with a hopeful conclusion that calls the reader to act.

lessons.title: Reading: Samina Khayal Baig — Pakistani Female Mountaineer
lessons.notes_html:
Who Is Samina Khayal Baig?

A mountaineer is a climber of mountains — a person who climbs mountains as a sport or profession. Samina Khayal Baig is a famous Pakistani female mountaineer from Shimshal village in Hunza, Gilgit-Baltistan. She is the first Pakistani female mountaineer to reach the top of K2, the third Pakistani to climb Mount Everest, and the youngest Muslim woman to climb Everest (at the age of 21). She is also the only Pakistani woman to have scaled the Seven Summits.

Her Distinguishing Achievements

  • First Pakistani woman to climb K2 (8611 metres, the world's 2nd highest peak).
  • Third Pakistani and youngest Muslim woman to climb Mount Everest (2013).
  • Only Pakistani woman to scale all Seven Summits in seven continents in just eight months.
  • In February 2018, the UNDP appointed her its goodwill ambassador for Pakistan to help fight climate change, poverty and inequality.

A Professional Climber

To be a professional means to do an activity as one's trained, full-time job or career, with proper training and skill, and to earn one's living by it. Samina Baig was trained in mountaineering from the age of 15 by her brother, Mirza Ali, and has been a professional climber since 2009, working as a mountain guide and expedition leader in the Hindu Kush, the Himalayas and the Karakoram.

Family Support and Gender Equality

Her brother climbed with her; on the Everest expedition he stopped about 248 metres short of the summit and let her go to the top on her own, to give a message of empowerment to all women of Pakistan. Gender equality means that men and women should have equal rights, respect and opportunities. Samina stated that her Everest expedition was a demonstration of gender equality.

The Scary Denali Climb

Climbing Denali (6194 metres) in Alaska was her most difficult and scary climb: her team was caught in a sudden snowstorm despite a clear forecast. They had no porters, carried their own gear, set up camp themselves, and were stuck in camp for five days with just three days of food supplies left.

A Role Model

Because of her, girls in Upper Hunza are now playing football and cricket and undertaking skiing, rock climbing, trekking and biking. She has set a trend that others can emulate. Women today have more education, more freedom and role models like her, though hurdles still exist.

Key Points

  • First Pakistani woman on K2 and Everest (youngest Muslim woman, age 21).
  • Only Pakistani woman to scale the Seven Summits — in eight months.
  • Trained by her brother Mirza Ali from age 15; professional since 2009.
  • UNDP goodwill ambassador for Pakistan since February 2018.

Word Meanings (Glossary)

  • mountaineer: a climber of mountains. peak: a mountain; summit.

lessons.title: Grammar: Punctuation
lessons.notes_html:
Where Punctuation Is Needed

  • Commas in a list: I bought some balloons, a cake and some ice cream for the party. He painted the fence white, blue and green.
  • Comma after Yes/No: No, I don't mind it. Yes, I love to go to the beach with my family.
  • Exclamation mark for strong feeling: Wow! Look at that.
  • Semicolon / dash between closely joined sentences: You cannot compete with him; he is a fast runner. Men were shouting, women were screaming, children were crying — it was chaos.
  • Quotation marks for spoken words: The teacher said, 'Open your books.' My father said, 'Always speak the truth.'
  • Question mark: Which one did you like the best?
  • Capital letters for proper nouns and the pronoun 'I': My mother and I went to Quetta. The Eiffel Tower, 300 metres high, is made of iron.
  • Apostrophe: My brother's name is on the merit list.

The 'Rainbows' Paragraph Punctuated

"My heart leaps up when I behold a rainbow in the sky," wrote William Wordsworth, the famous poet, and most of us share his feelings when we are lucky enough to see a rainbow. There is an old saying that a pot of gold is buried at the end of the rainbow, but have you ever tried to reach a rainbow's end? Of course, it's impossible, because a rainbow is really just the result of the raindrops refracting and reflecting light. There are seven colours in the rainbow: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet.

Key Points

  • Every sentence begins with a capital letter and ends with a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark.
  • Use commas to separate items in a list and after introductory Yes/No.
  • Put spoken words inside quotation marks, with a comma before them.

lessons.title: Grammar: The Present Perfect Tense — has/have and for/since
lessons.notes_html:
The Present Perfect Simple Tense

The present perfect is formed with has/have + the third form of the verb (past participle). Use has with he, she, it and singular nouns; use have with I, we, you, they and plural nouns.

  • We have bought a computer. I have completed my homework. You have worked here for a year.
  • He has scored two goals. She has learnt three languages. The world population has increased rapidly.
  • The pace of life has become (not became) faster. The scientists have found more energy sources.

For and Since

We use 'for' when we mention the length of the period, and 'since' when we mention the starting point of the period.

  • for: for 10 years; for 6 years; for three weeks; for a month.
  • since: since last Monday; since Friday; since 2009; since March; since times immemorial (the starting point).
  • She has taught in the school for 10 years. He has climbed three peaks since 2009. I have not seen him since last Monday.

Key Points

  • After has/have, always use the third form: become, found, bought, learnt.
  • Ask yourself: is it a length of time (for) or a starting point (since)?

Chronological Order

The book asks for an essay on a Pakistani sports personality using chronological (sequential) order — arranging details in the order of time, from the earliest events to the latest achievements.

Model Essay (Samina Baig)

Samina Khayal Baig was born on 19th September 1990 in Shimshal village, Hunza, Gilgit-Baltistan. She was trained in mountaineering from the age of 15 by her brother Mirza Ali, and she has been a professional climber since 2009, working as a mountain guide and expedition leader. In 2013, she became the first Pakistani woman to climb Mount Everest, at the age of 21. In the next eight months she scaled the highest peaks of all seven continents — Aconcagua, Vinson Massif, Kilimanjaro, Puncak Jaya, Denali and Elbrus. Later she also reached the top of K2, the second highest peak in the world. In February 2018, the UNDP appointed her its goodwill ambassador for Pakistan. Through her courage and hard work, Samina Baig has proved that Pakistani women can achieve anything, and she remains a role model for the youth.

Key Points

  • Begin with birth and early life; end with the latest honour.
  • Use time expressions to guide the reader: 'In 2013...', 'In the next eight months...', 'Later...', 'In February 2018...'.
  • Keep every event in its correct time order — do not jump back and forth.

lessons.title: Reading: Review of Units 4–6
lessons.notes_html:
Matching Words with Meanings

  • summit — the highest point of a mountain. peak — pointed top of a mountain.
  • particle — a minute portion of matter. lucrative — profitable.
  • ambassador — representative. emission — discharge (giving out of smoke/gas).
  • smog — mixture of smoke and fog. mountaineering — activity of climbing mountains.
  • despite — in spite of. incredible — unbelievable.

Questions from the Units

  • Jinnah described Hindus and Muslims as two separate nations because they belonged to two different religious philosophies, social customs and traditions, could not intermarry, and belonged to two different civilizations based on conflicting ideas.
  • The Quaid asked Muslims to resolve their differences so they could unite on one platform with a common bond with the Muslim League; only a united nation could win freedom.
  • Every winter the cities in the upper and central parts of Pakistan wear a blanket of fog, which pollutants thicken into smog. To avoid smog's effects: use a face mask, drink extra water, wash hands and face indoors, avoid going out unnecessarily, seal windows, use air purifiers, and drive slowly with fog lights.
  • To be a professional means to practise an activity as one's trained, full-time career and earn one's living by it — Samina Baig has been a professional climber since 2009.
  • Samina Baig encourages the youth as a role model: her Everest success encouraged girls to take up climbing and other sports in Upper Hunza.

Oral Communication

Useful model answers: study skills are the methods we use to learn well — making a timetable, revising daily, taking notes and avoiding distractions. Patriotism is love for one's country; we serve our nation by studying honestly, obeying the law, keeping our surroundings clean and becoming useful citizens. The internet is the best source for a weather forecast because it is updated every hour.

lessons.title: Vocabulary and Grammar: for/since, Word Pairs, Dictation and Punctuation
lessons.notes_html:
For and Since — More Practice

  • I have not heard from them since I was six. (starting point)
  • It has not rained for two months. They have been waiting for 35 minutes.
  • You have not changed since the last time I saw you. My sister has been studying for two hours.
  • I have not seen you for ages. She has been training for two weeks.
  • We had been struggling for a separate homeland for several years.
  • You have not phoned your family since you left home. Man has struggled against nature since times immemorial.

Pairs of Words with Different Meanings

  • peak / peek: K2 is the second highest peak in the world. / She took a quick peek at the gift.
  • hoard / horde: Some people hoard food in times of shortage. / A horde of tourists visited the fort.
  • advice / advise: My teacher gave me good advice. (noun) / I advise you to work hard. (verb)
  • moral / morale: The story teaches us a moral lesson. / The victory raised the morale of the team.
  • adopt / adapt: They decided to adopt good study habits. / Plants adapt themselves to the climate.
  • accept / except: Please accept my invitation. / Everyone came except Ali.

Dictation Words

ceaseless, unreflective, achievement, ambassador, mountaineer, Karakoram, separate, conference, fulfilment, illiteracy, purchase, exemplary.

Punctuating a Story Opening

"One day a farmer went with his oxen to plough his field. He had just turned the first furrow when a tiger walked up and said, 'Peace be with you, friend. How are you this fine morning?' 'The same to you, my lord, and I am pretty well, thank you,' replied the farmer, quaking with fear but thinking it wisest to be polite."

Key Points

  • 'For' measures how long; 'since' points to when it began — even with phrases like 'ages' (for) and 'times immemorial' (since).
  • Advice is the noun; advise is the verb.

lessons.notes_html:
The Model Essay (An Inspirational Leader)

Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah is an inspirational leader for every Pakistani. He was a man of principle, a brilliant lawyer and a devoted, untiring worker. When the Muslims of India were scattered and hopeless, he united them on one platform, awakened them from their sleep, and led them with wisdom and courage. He never used unfair means and never gave up, even in poor health. As a result of his ceaseless struggle, Pakistan appeared on the map of the world on 14th August 1947. His life teaches us that honesty, unity, faith and discipline can achieve even the most difficult goals. That is why he will always remain an inspiration for the nation.

The Alternative Topic

Key Points

  • An essay on a person should move from introduction → qualities and struggle → result → lesson for us.
  • Support every quality with an action: 'devoted worker' — he worked even in poor health.
  • End by telling what the leader's life teaches us today.

lessons.title: Reading: Eid-ul-Adha
lessons.notes_html:
Two Eids in a Year

Muslims celebrate two Eids in a year: Eid-ul-Fitr, which comes at the end of Ramadan, and Eid-ul-Adha, which takes place about two months after Eid-ul-Fitr, on the 10th of Zilhajj, at the end of the annual Hajj. Eidi (money or gifts from elders) is most commonly given on Eid-ul-Fitr, though many families also give it on Eid-ul-Adha; on Eid-ul-Adha the greater joy is in sharing the meat of the sacrificed animal with family, friends and the needy.

The Festival of Sacrifice

Eid-ul-Adha is the festival of sacrifice. 'Adha' is an Arabic word which means 'sacrifice'. In a dream, Allah commanded Hazrat Ibrahim (AS) to sacrifice his son Hazrat Ismail (AS). Satan tried to tempt him not to obey, but he drove Satan away. Allah sent the angel Jibrail (AS) with a ram to sacrifice instead of his son. The saving of Hazrat Ismail (AS) was a miracle — a wonderful event that cannot be explained by the laws of nature and is done by the power of Allah — which proved that He has command over all things, the known and the unknown.

Eid-ul-Fitr and Eid-ul-Adha Compared

  • Eid-ul-Fitr occurs at the end of Ramadan — the month in which the first verses of the Holy Quran were revealed — and marks the end of fasting.
  • Eid-ul-Adha is on the 10th of Zilhajj at the end of Hajj, and animals are sacrificed in memory of Hazrat Ibrahim's (AS) sacrifice. This sacrifice of animals differentiates the two festivals.
  • On Eid-ul-Adha, Muslims sacrifice a lamb, goat, cow, camel or other halal animal, following the Sunnah of Hazrat Ibrahim (AS).

Showing Firm Belief on Eid

A Muslim shows firm belief in Allah on Eid days by obeying His commands sincerely: he performs ghusl, wears new clean clothes, uses miswak, applies scent, reaches the place of prayer early (the Sunnahs of Eid day), offers the communal Eid namaz, and on Eid-ul-Adha sacrifices an animal and shares its meat with family, friends and the needy. The lesson of Eid-ul-Adha is complete obedience and submission to Allah — sacrificing even what we love most — and sharing our blessings with the needy.

Point of View

In first-person writing the narrator uses I, my, me, we, our, us: "I wandered lonely as a cloud." "Much to my surprise, I liked the truck." In third-person writing the narrator tells about others — he, she, they, their: "She wanted to play cricket." "Maria was sure to get first position in her class." "They did not lose heart and kept on their journey."

Oral Communication

In the book's dialogue, Ali tells Hamza about the Kelantan International Wau Festival in Malaysia, held annually in August; a 'wau' is a huge kite decorated with colourful patterns of flowers and leaves. His favourite food there was 'Nasi Tumpang' — rice packed in a cone-shaped banana leaf.

Key Points

  • Adha = sacrifice; the festival commemorates Hazrat Ibrahim's (AS) readiness to sacrifice his son.
  • The ram sent through Jibrail (AS) replaced Hazrat Ismail (AS) — a miracle of Allah.
  • First person = I/we; third person = he/she/they.

lessons.title: Vocabulary: Word Meanings and Near Homophones
lessons.notes_html:
Word Meanings (Glossary)

  • festival: a time of celebration. approaching: drawing nearer.
  • command: to order. celebrate: to mark or observe an event.
  • commemoration: a celebration in memory of a person or event.
  • sacrificial: relating to sacrifice. environment: all surrounding things.
  • clarify: to make clear. calendar: a system for organizing days and months of the year.
  • differentiate: to see the difference between two or more things.

More Dictionary Meanings

  • tempt: to try to persuade someone to do something wrong.
  • sacrifice: to give up something valuable for a noble cause; the killing of an animal as an offering to Allah.
  • communal: shared by a whole community; done together. reveal: to make known; to show something hidden.
  • belief: firm faith; trust in something true. forgiveness: the act of pardoning someone.

Near Homophones — Choosing the Correct Word

  • than / then: than introduces a comparison (taller than his father); then means next, in that time (First he sent a message, then he called).
  • affect / effect: affect is a verb = to make a difference (The cold weather began to affect his emotions); effect is a noun = a result (the effect of soil erosion).
  • lose / loose: lose = to fail or be unable to find (I hope we don't lose the game); loose = free, not tight (a dog running loose).
  • since / sense: since = because, or from a time (waiting since noon); sense = a feeling or faculty (Nabila had a sense that something was wrong).
  • and / an: and joins two things (Shakespeare and Mark Twain); an comes before a vowel sound (an owl).

Key Points

  • Remember: affect = verb (action), effect = noun (result).
  • Use the meaning of the sentence to choose between look-alike words.

lessons.title: Grammar: The Order of Adjectives
lessons.notes_html:
The Correct Order of Adjectives

When several adjectives come before a noun, they follow this order: number → opinion → size → shape → age → condition → colour → pattern → origin → material → purpose.

  • an orange, cotton shirt (colour before material)
  • a beautiful, old woman (opinion before age)
  • an amazing, Floridian sunset (opinion before origin)
  • twelve medium, shampoo bottles (number, size, purpose)
  • two square, blue tables (number, shape, colour)
  • a delicious Italian meal (opinion before origin)
  • a stinky, bathroom towel (opinion/condition before purpose)
  • an ugly, old, yellow bus (opinion, age, colour)
  • a pretty, large blanket (opinion before size)
  • five empty trunks (number before condition); three fun games (number before opinion)

Describing Pictures in the Correct Order

  • It is a round, blue and black football. (shape, colour)
  • It is a big, green, shady tree. (size, colour)
  • It is a new, red, sports car. (age, colour, purpose)
  • It is a large, green, juicy watermelon. (size, colour)
  • It is a long, yellow, wooden pencil. (size, colour, material)

Key Points

  • Number always comes first: 'three fun games', not 'fun three games'.
  • Opinion comes before facts like size, age and colour: 'a pretty, large blanket'.
  • Material and purpose come last, closest to the noun: 'a wooden pencil', 'a bathroom towel'.

lessons.title: Writing: Analogies and Dialogue Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Analogies

An analogy shows the relationship between two objects or concepts. First find the relationship in the first pair, then apply the same relationship to the second pair. "Blue is to the sky as green is to grass."

  • An apple is to fruit as a carrot is to vegetable. (kind/class)
  • Toe is to foot as finger is to hand. Brother is to boy as sister is to girl. (part/family relation)
  • A bird is to a feather as a fish is to a scale. (covering)
  • Morning is to breakfast as evening is to dinner. (meal of the time)
  • A hat is to head as a shoe is to foot. A straw is to drink as a spoon is to eat. (use)
  • The moon is to night as the sun is to day. A car is to a road as a boat is to water. (place of working)
  • A hammer is to a nail as a comb is to hair. A sculptor is to a stone as a chef is to food. (tool/worker and object)
  • White is to black as up is to down. (opposites)

Writing a Dialogue

The book's model dialogue is between two friends on the choice of a career. Ahmed wishes to join the Pakistan Army as an officer to defend his country like the martyrs; Bilal wants to become a doctor to serve the sick people of his village. They agree that the important thing is to work hard and be honest in whichever career they choose. A good dialogue has greetings, natural questions and answers, clear reasons, and a proper closing.

Key Points

  • For an analogy, name the relationship first: kind, part, use, place, opposite.
  • In a dialogue, give each speaker a name, keep turns short, and end with a conclusion or farewell.

lessons.title: Reading: The Wise Old Woman
lessons.notes_html:
The Cruel Decree

The young lord of the village was arrogant and cruel. He decreed (gave a formal order) that anyone over seventy-one must be banished from the village and left in the mountains to die, because, in his words, old people were "neither useful nor able to work for a living." When the farmer's mother turned seventy, he sadly took her to the mountain, as the decree ordered.

The Mother's Love

On the way, the mother kept breaking off small twigs to mark the path so that her son would not get lost while returning. Seeing that even at the time of her own death she was thinking only of him, the farmer could bear it no longer. He brought her back home and hid her in a secret room he dug in the floor of his kitchen, carrying meals to her there for almost two years.

Lord Higa's Three Impossible Demands

Lord Higa, the powerful lord of the town beyond the hills, threatened to attack the village and make it his own if his demands were not met. The village's wise men could solve none of them and only shook their heads, which made the young lord angry: "What good is your wisdom if you cannot help me now?" The hidden old woman solved all three with her wisdom and experience:

  • One thousand ropes of ash: soak ordinary rope in salt water, dry it well, then burn it — it holds its shape as a rope of ash.
  • Threading a silk thread through a bent log: put sugar at one end of the hole and tie an ant to a silk thread at the other end; the ant weaves through the curves to the sugar, taking the thread with it.
  • A drum that sounds without being beaten: make a drum with sides of paper and put a bumblebee inside; as it tries to escape, it buzzes and beats against the paper, making the drum sound.

The Lord Learns His Lesson

When the lord learnt that the hidden old mother had solved all three problems and saved the village, he realised his mistake. He admitted he had been very wrong, asked forgiveness of the mother and of all his people, and promised that old people would never again be sent to the mountains, but would be treated with respect and honour.

Main Idea

The main idea of the story is that old people are not useless; their wisdom and experience are a treasure for the young. The wise old woman saved the whole village three times, and the young lord learnt to treat old people with the respect and honour they deserve.

Oral Communication

In the book's role-play, a mother explains the recipe of fried rice step by step — using the sequence words First, Then, Next, Finally: heat oil, add garlic, onions and salt; add rice and fry; add peas and eggs; fry about 15 minutes; add pepper and tomato sauce; serve garnished with spring onions and chillies.

Key Points

  • The decree: everyone over seventy-one to be banished to the mountains.
  • The mother's twigs on the path showed her selfless love.
  • Wisdom and experience, not strength, saved the village.

lessons.title: Reading: Fact or Opinion and 'The Simpsons' Paragraph
lessons.notes_html:
Fact and Opinion

A fact is something that can be proved true. An opinion is a personal feeling or judgement that cannot be proved. Words like 'I think', 'best', 'better' and 'most exciting' usually signal an opinion.

  • Facts: Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah was the first Governor General of Pakistan. The scientific name of the domestic cat is Felis catus. Young cats are called kittens. A bowling ball has three holes in it.
  • Opinions: I think cats make the best pets! The slide is the most exciting part of the playground. Mosquitoes are the most annoying insects. Football is better than cricket.

'The Simpsons' Paragraph — Questions Answered

  • 'The Simpsons' is a cartoon series.
  • Bart, Lisa and Maggie are brother and sisters.
  • Synonym of 'perfect' — ideal. Synonym of 'long' — lengthy. Synonym of 'vegetarian' — herbivorous.
  • Antonym of 'active' — lazy. Antonym of 'disobedient' — obedient. Antonym of 'smart' — stupid.

Key Points

  • A fact can be checked and proved; an opinion expresses a feeling.
  • A synonym is a word with a similar meaning; an antonym has the opposite meaning.

options: I think cats make the best pets!

options: The slide is the most exciting part of the playground.

lessons.title: Vocabulary: Figures of Speech, Idioms and Proverbs
lessons.notes_html:
Figures of Speech

  • Simile — compares two unlike things using 'like' or 'as': Hamza is as brave as a lion. Maria is like an angel. Life is like a box of chocolates. Her eyes were like diamonds.
  • Metaphor — describes one thing as another: The pen is mightier than the sword. The house was a zoo.
  • Personification — gives human traits to non-living things: You can hear the trees whisper in the dark. The window panes were talking as the wind blew.
  • Hyperbole — extreme exaggeration: It costs an arm and a leg. This is the best book ever written.
  • Onomatopoeia — words that imitate natural sounds: The car horn beeped loudly. My teeth chattered. The leaves crunched under my feet.
  • A plain statement like "The sun is shining brightly" has no figure of speech.

Idioms

  • I am feeling blue — I am sad. I am in a pickle — I am in trouble.
  • Don't give me the cold shoulder — Don't ignore me. That's a piece of cake — That is easy.
  • Please give me a hand — Please help. My eyes are bigger than my stomach — I take more food than I can eat.
  • They have buried the hatchet — They have ended a quarrel. Once in a blue moon — very rarely.

Proverbs

  • No pain, no gain — Achievements require some sort of sacrifice.
  • Actions speak louder than words — What a person actually does is more important than what he says he will do.
  • A stitch in time saves nine — It is better to deal with a problem at an early stage to prevent it from getting worse.
  • Rome was not built in a day — It takes a long time to do a job properly.
  • Birds of a feather flock together — People of the same sort are usually found together.

Syllables

basketball — 3 — bas/ket/ball. offering — 3 — of/fer/ing. bewilderment — 4 — be/wil/der/ment. villagers — 3 — vil/la/gers. farmer — 2 — far/mer. beautiful — 3 — beau/ti/ful. elephant — 3 — el/e/phant.

Key Points

  • Look for 'like' or 'as' to spot a simile; a metaphor says one thing IS another.
  • An idiom's meaning cannot be guessed from its separate words.

lessons.title: Writing: Word Building with -able/-ible and Dialogue Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Words with -able, -ible, -ably, -ibly

  • -able: comfortable, washable, readable, eatable, lovable. (Example in the book: unable.)
  • -ible: edible, audible, visible, possible, sensible. (Example: invisible.)
  • -ably: comfortably, reasonably, suitably, remarkably, honourably. (Example: acceptably.)
  • -ibly: possibly, sensibly, terribly, visibly, audibly. (Example: terribly.)

A Model Dialogue: Doctor and Patient

The patient complains of stomach pain and tiredness. The doctor finds that junk food and irregular meals have upset his stomach. He gives medicine for the pain but insists: "Medicine alone will not help. You must take a healthy diet — fresh vegetables, fruits, milk and home-cooked food — and avoid oily and fast food." With a healthy diet and regular exercise, the patient will avoid such problems in the future.

Key Points

  • There is no single rule for -able/-ible; learn the spellings word by word.
  • In a dialogue, the doctor asks, advises and insists politely; the patient answers and promises to follow the advice.

chapters.title: Unit 9 — Think Not All is Over (Poem)

lessons.title: Reading: Think Not All is Over
lessons.notes_html:
The Message of the Poem

The title 'Think Not All is Over' suggests that the poem is about hope. It tells us not to think that everything has ended when we are in trouble; bad times will pass and good times will return. The poetess, Harriet Beecher Stowe, has implicit faith in God's love and mercy. The poetess repeats the negative command 'Think not' at the start of the stanzas, but she uses it to remove despair, not to create it: "Think not all is over" means "do not lose hope".

Every Sad Situation Has a Hopeful Side

  • After the autumn winds drive away the leaves, 'spring returneth' and we see 'buds and leaves and blossoms' again.
  • When the earth lies cold and the birds mourn, 'God still liveth' and 'songs and sunshine shall again return'.
  • When the heart is sad and hopes are dead, 'God still loveth' and 'He will wipe away thy every tear'.
  • 'Weeping for a night alone endureth; God at last shall bring a morning hour.'
  • 'In the frozen buds of every winter sleep the blossoms of a future flower.'

Pathetic Fallacy

Pathetic fallacy is a figure of speech in which nature or non-living things are given human feelings and emotions. Examples in the first stanza: 'the wailing winds of autumn' — the winds are shown crying like a grieving human; and 'the shivering leaflets' — the little leaves are shown trembling like a frightened or cold person.

Symbols of Sadness

Words and images of sadness in the poem: 'wailing winds of autumn', 'shivering leaflets', the earth lying 'cold and sealed', the 'weary birds' that 'mourn', the heart that is 'waste and dreary', 'cherished hopes' lying 'chill and sere' (dry and dead), 'weeping' and 'tears', and the 'frozen buds of winter'.

Word Meanings

  • wailing: crying with pain, grief or anger. shiver: shake, tremble.
  • blossom: flower. shalt: shall. weary: very tired or bored.
  • dreary: dull and making you feel sad. cherished: dear; loved and protected.
  • endure: to tolerate; to bear patiently. leaflet: a small leaf. chill: cold.

How to Behave in a Problem

When we face a problem, we should stay calm and patient, pray to Allah, think about possible solutions, take advice from our elders, and keep trying instead of losing hope — because, as the poem teaches, sorrow lasts only for a night and God brings the morning hour.

Key Points

  • The poem's message: never lose hope; spring follows winter.
  • Pathetic fallacy gives human feelings to nature.
  • The negative form 'Think not' carries a positive, hopeful message.

lessons.title: Vocabulary and Grammar: Homographs and Degrees of Adjectives
lessons.notes_html:
Homographs

Homographs are words that have the same spelling but different pronunciation and meaning. The unit practises: row (a line / to quarrel), wind (moving air / to turn), record (a written account / to write down), present (a gift / to show), tear (a drop from the eye), close (near).

  • You have to wind (turn) the handle to the left. / Wind speeds reached 102 mph last night.
  • I looked along the row (line) of books. / We do not row (quarrel) about the money.
  • There was a tear in the corner of his eye.
  • Please keep close (near) to the path.
  • Keep a record (written account) of your expenses. / Make sure you record (write down) the date.
  • The watch was a present (gift) from my mother. / Please present (show) your boarding card at the gate.

Degrees of Adjectives

  • great — greater — greatest. small — smaller — smallest. rich — richer — richest. poor — poorer — poorest.
  • happy — happier — happiest (y changes to i). wealthy — wealthier — wealthiest.
  • beautiful — more beautiful — most beautiful. cherished — more cherished — most cherished.
  • One- or two-syllable adjectives add -er and -est; adjectives of more than two syllables take 'more' and 'most'; irregular ones change completely (good–better–best, bad–worse–worst); absolute adjectives like unique, perfect, round have no degrees.

Key Points

  • For homographs, read the sentence's meaning to know which word is meant.
  • Short adjectives take -er/-est; long adjectives take more/most.

options: Sound the same but are spelt differently

lessons.title: Writing: Paraphrasing a Poem
lessons.notes_html:
What Is a Paraphrase?

A paraphrase restates a poem or passage in our own simple words, keeping the meaning complete. The book's task is to paraphrase the first two stanzas of 'Think Not All is Over', beginning: "Harriet Beecher Stowe, the poetess, has implicit faith in God's love and …"

Model Paraphrase

"Harriet Beecher Stowe, the poetess, has implicit faith in God's love and mercy. She says that when the sad winds of autumn blow and drive the trembling little leaves from the trees, we should not think that everything is finished, because spring will come back and we shall again see buds, leaves and flowers. In the same way, when the earth lies cold and closed in winter and the tired birds seem to mourn above it, we should not think that all is over, because God is still alive, and the songs of birds and the sunshine will surely return again."

Key Points

  • A paraphrase keeps every idea of the original but uses simple, own words.
  • It is written in prose, in the third person, and does not add new ideas.
  • Figures of speech are explained plainly: 'wailing winds' become 'the sad winds'.

lessons.title: Reading Review: Figures of Speech, Fact or Opinion, Nepal
lessons.notes_html:
Figures of Speech — Review Answers

  • Similes: He is as brave as a lion. Her hair was as dark as night. Doing homework is like doing chores. My tea was like hot lava. Experience is like a teacher. Soldiers were like lions in the fight.
  • Metaphors: I am a rock, strong and hard. The camel is called the ship of the desert. She is a cuckoo.
  • Personification: The cookies begged me to eat them. The wind was moaning and flowers were tossing their heads. The sun is playing hide-and-seek with the clouds.

Fact or Opinion — Review Answers

  • Facts: Bats are nocturnal mammals. Snow is white. Rain falls from the clouds. A plane is faster than a car. Brazil is located in the continent of South America. Quaid-e-Azam was the first Governor General of Pakistan.
  • Opinions: I think it will rain today. My school is the best school ever. Rainy days are boring. White is my favourite colour.

The Nepal Paragraph — Answers

  • Nepal is situated between China and India.
  • Mount Everest is situated in Nepal. The capital of Nepal is Kathmandu.
  • The plains in the southern part are called the Terai region.
  • Nepal can be divided into three regions.

Oral Communication — Eid Day

In the model discussion, Eid Day begins with ghusl, new clothes and Eid namaz; the sacrificed goat's meat is divided into three parts — one for the family, one for relatives and friends, and one for the needy. Eid Day teaches sharing, sacrifice and thankfulness to Allah.

Key Points

  • 'Best school ever' and 'favourite colour' are opinions — they cannot be proved.
  • Nepal: capital Kathmandu, Everest, Terai plains, three regions.

Key Points
