lessons.title: Reading: The Young Boy's Adventure
lessons.notes_html:
The Father — Herschel

The boy's father, whom most people called Herschel, was the owner of the Glenn Plumbing Company. Although the company grew into a successful business, he recognised the limitations of his education and wanted his son to gain curiosity and learning. He could turn very serious at times, but most of the time he was light-hearted; he joked a lot and made his son laugh. He was curious about things, always wanted to learn new things himself, and would go out of his way to investigate them. He was progressive and eager to experiment.

The Adventure

The father went to Cambridge — the town in America (Ohio) near which the boy lived, not the city in England — to check on a plumbing job of his company. On the way back they stopped at a grass-field airport. The dad had wanted to see what flying felt like ever since he had been in France in World War I and had seen biplanes dogfighting over the lines — that is, for many years. Charles Lindbergh ('Lindy'), the famous pilot who crossed the Atlantic Ocean in a solo flight two years before, was their inspiration.

The Plane and the Flight

The plane was an old open-cockpit biplane — an old-fashioned airplane with two sets of wings — bigger than the boy had thought, with two cockpits, one in front and one behind. The back seat was wide enough for father and son, with one strap across them both, though the boy could barely see out. When the boy (Bud) saw a silver plane flying west overhead, he wanted to go up in it: "I probably was scared at the idea of going up, but there wasn't any doubt about it — I wanted to do it."

During the flight the boy was thrilled and elated (extremely happy). The plane bounced down the grass strip and rose; it banked and he could look straight down; he felt suspended without falling, and everything on the ground looked small, like the buildings and trees in a toy train set. He could not catch his dad's words over the sound of the engine and the rushing air. As they drove home, Dad asked if he had liked the flight; the boy said he had, and the father said he had liked it too.

The Lesson of the Story

The most important lesson of the boy's youth was his father's eagerness to experiment: flying was not simply fun for his father; he wanted to experience it himself so that he could speak with authority about what it felt like. Curiosity and learning by first-hand experience give real understanding and confidence.

Word Meanings

  • curious: wanting to know; eager to know. curiosity: the desire to know about something.
  • plumbing: the job of fitting and repairing pipes, water tanks etc. cockpit: the part of the plane where the pilot sits.
  • biplane: an old-fashioned airplane with two sets of wings. transatlantic: across the Atlantic Ocean (of a flight).
  • dogfight: a fight between armed aircraft. elated: extremely happy. adventure: an exciting and unusual experience or journey.
  • unbounded: without any limit. barely: only just. goggles: special glasses used when swimming and flying. progressive: supporting new or modern ideas.

Oral Communication — Listening Skills

The book's dialogue teaches that listening is the most fundamental component of communication skills; active listening gives the other person time to express thoughts and feelings, builds lifelong friendships and develops patience; 'taking turns' means when one person speaks, the other listens, and we should not interrupt.

Key Points

  • Herschel: light-hearted, curious, progressive — owner of Glenn Plumbing Company.
  • A biplane has two sets of wings; dogfighting is combat between armed aircraft.
  • The story's lesson: learn by first-hand experience.

lessons.title: Grammar: Modal Verbs
lessons.notes_html:
Choosing the Suitable Modal Verb — The Book's Answers

  • My father would drink tea daily at night. (would — a past habit)
  • You need to buy a big bag.
  • I could row the boat, but I did not. (could — past ability, unused)
  • She said that he might wait for her. (might — past of may in reported speech)
  • We shall go there tomorrow.
  • You need not stay long there.
  • You must brush your teeth daily. (must — strong duty)
  • He ought to quit smoking. (ought to — moral duty/advice)
  • He did not dare to call me. (dare — courage)

Key Points

  • would = past habit; could = past ability; might = reported/weak possibility.
  • must and ought to show duty; need not shows there is no necessity.
  • Modal verbs are followed by the base form of the main verb.

lessons.title: Vocabulary and Writing: Abbreviations, Acronyms and Letter Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Abbreviations (Short Forms of Words)

  • adj. = adjective, adjectival; adj. phrase = adjectival phrase; adjs. = adjectives; adv. = adverb, adverbial.
  • Dec. = December; Dept. = department; Govt. = government; Gr. = grammar; Mon. = Monday; Dr = Doctor.

Acronyms (First Letters, Pronounced as One Word)

  • CAP = Community Access Point. NASA = National Aeronautics and Space Administration.
  • ADA = American Dental Association. PARCO = Pak-Arab Oil Refinery Company.
  • CED = Central Excise Duty. NAB = National Accountability Bureau.
  • OPEC = Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries. WASA = Water and Sanitation Authority.

Writing a Formal Letter

The book's task: write a letter to your friend asking him to join as a manager in your company, giving two reasons why he would be a suitable candidate. In the model letter, Naeem Mansoor (Director) invites Mr Kamran Ahmed to join City Textiles as Manager for two reasons: (1) he has five years of experience in managing a sales team with an excellent record of meeting targets; (2) he is well known for his honesty, hard work and pleasant dealing with customers and staff. A formal letter carries the address, a courteous opening, a clear purpose, reasons in the body, and a polite closing ('Cordially').

Key Points

  • An abbreviation shortens a word; an acronym is pronounced as a word (NASA, NAB).
  • In the model letter, the two reasons are experience and character (honesty and hard work).

lessons.title: Reading: Pakistani Culture
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Culture?

Culture consists of the way of life, language, ideas, beliefs, customs, codes, institutions, tools, techniques, works of arts and ceremonies of a particular country. In Allama Iqbal's words, "Culture encompasses all the mental, spiritual and physical activities of a nation. It includes the basic beliefs and faith, values and literature, art and architecture, music and mode of dress, manners and customs prevalent in a given society."

Unity in Diversity

Pakistan has four main provincial cultures — Punjabi, Sindhi, Balochi and Pashtun (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa). They differ in language, dress, food, sports and festivals, yet they are united because Pakistani culture is primarily based on the Islamic way of life. Pakistan is an ideological Islamic state, so all ingredients of our culture are inspired by Islam — for example, Muslims eat halal food. Pakistani culture is highlighted by its grandeur yet simplicity, firm convictions, noble deeds and ideas.

Punjab

  • Punjabi is the provincial language of Punjab, spoken as a first language by 44% of Pakistanis; Urdu too is commonly spoken in this region.
  • Punjabi people are fond of kabaddi and wrestling; other games include gilli danda, kho-kho, yassu-panju, pitho-garam, baraf-panni, ludo, chuppan-chupai and kanchy, and major sports include cricket, boxing, horse-racing, polo, hockey and football.
  • Punjabi poetry is renowned for its deep meaning, beautiful and hopeful insight; Sufi literature is very popular. Famous poets: Sultan Bahu, Mian Muhammad Bakhsh, Baba Farid, Shah Hussain and Anwar Masood. Waris Shah, best known for 'Heer Ranjha', is called the Shakespeare of Punjab; Bulleh Shah was a Punjabi Sufi poet, humanist and philosopher.

Sindh, Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa

  • The people of interior Sindh have an agricultural-based lifestyle; the fertile Indus plains support farming, and inland fishing is practised along the Indus River. Traditional dishes include Pallo Machi (fish), Palli (leafy green), Bhee (lotus root), phulka and rice.
  • Baloch people celebrate religious festivals like Eid-ul-Fitr and Eid-ul-Adha and many social festivals, like the Sibi festival with folk music, cultural dances, handicrafts stalls and cattle shows.
  • Pathans (Pashtuns) are famous for their poetry; they are passionate and patriotic. Famous poets: Amir Kror Suri, Khushal Khan Khattak and Rahman Baba. Famous KP dishes: tikkah, suji ka halwa, kehwa, chapali kabab, kabali palao and special long naans.

Word Meanings

  • custom: something done traditionally in a society. ceremony: a public or religious occasion with formal actions. spiritual: connected with the human spirit.
  • ingredient: one of the things from which something is made. conviction: a strong opinion or belief. aspect: a particular part or feature.
  • heterogeneous: consisting of many different kinds. shrine: a place of homage connected with a holy person or event. encompass: to include all or a large number of things.
  • deeds: actions. clans: large families or tribes. costumes: sets of clothes for an occasion or group. urban: relating to a city or town. cuisine: the style of cooking of a place.

Key Points

  • The main idea: Pakistan's four cultures differ in many ways yet are united by Islam — unity in diversity.
  • Waris Shah = Shakespeare of Punjab; Sibi = famous Baloch festival.

lessons.title: Grammar: Sentence Patterns, Keywords, Phrases and Clauses
lessons.notes_html:
Parts of a Sentence

  • Subject: 'We' in "We turned the pages." Verb: 'won' in "They won the match"; 'am' in "I am healthy."
  • Direct object — the object the verb acts on: 'the lesson' in "The students learnt the lesson"; 'a story' in "She told me a story."
  • Indirect object — the recipient of the direct object: 'me' in "My brother gave me a pen."
  • Complement — a word after a linking verb: 'happy' in "She is happy."
  • 'Greedily' in "He ate the chocolate greedily" is an adverb modifying the verb — not one of the five parts above; the direct object there is 'the chocolate'.

Sentence Patterns

  • S + V + O: Ali reads a book. The teacher praised the students. We planted a tree. She cooked rice. The cat chased the mouse.
  • S + V + DO + IO (book's example: She sent a message to me): He gave a gift to his friend. Mother baked a cake for us. The teacher told a story to the class. I wrote a letter to my uncle.

Keywords in a Question

Keywords are the important words — nouns, pronouns, verbs and question words; articles and prepositions are not keywords. Examples: "What did Margie write in her diary?" — Margie, write, diary. "Where was Margie's school?" — Where, Margie's school. "Why did they take online classes?" — Why, take, online classes. Note the verb tense too ('did write' = past), so the answer is given accordingly.

Phrases and Clauses

  • A phrase is two or more related words with no subject-verb pair: 'knocking at the door', 'While looking out of the window', 'for half an hour', 'very soon this evening', 'not ready', 'to save the drowning boy'.
  • A clause contains a subject and a verb: 'We could not open the door', 'She put the geometry box on the table', 'Put it here' (imperative; subject 'you' understood), 'You have no legal right to claim it', 'I saw a passenger with a heavy bag'.

Dependent Clauses

A dependent (subordinate) clause cannot stand alone and usually begins with which, that, who, when, if, before, after, because, unless: 'who appeared on screen' (We saw a teacher who appeared on screen); 'when you need help'; 'if you win this award'; 'before we left'; 'that I have to learn by heart'; 'when the game is over'. Note: "Look at the picture below the text" has NO dependent clause — 'below the text' is only a phrase.

Key Points

  • Direct object answers 'what?'; indirect object answers 'to/for whom?'.
  • No subject-verb pair = phrase; subject + verb = clause.

lessons.title: Grammar: The Future Perfect Tense
lessons.notes_html:
Form of the Future Perfect

Subject + will/shall have + past participle. The book's correct options: The farmer will have ploughed the field. They will win the match (base form after will in simple future). You will have arrived by then. The boy will have spent the money. They will have completed their homework. We shall have crossed the channel. You will have watched the documentary. She will have made a decision by then. I shall have reached the office. He will have received my gift.

Changing Sentences into the Future Perfect

  • They have built a grand house. → They will have built a grand house.
  • We had learnt many new things. → We shall have learnt many new things.
  • He has moved into his new house. → He will have moved into his new house.
  • They restored the power supply. → They will have restored the power supply.
  • She will paint the picture. → She will have painted the picture.
  • They repaired the road. → They will have repaired the road.
  • We have come back from the study tour. → We shall have come back from the study tour.
  • You have locked the door. → You will have locked the door.
  • (Book misprints corrected: 'I will have inform them' → I shall have informed them; 'We shall have win the match' → We shall have won the match — the past participles are 'informed' and 'won'.)

Key Points

  • After will/shall comes 'have' (never 'has') plus the past participle.
  • 'By then' is a common time marker of the future perfect.

lessons.title: Writing: Editing and Proofreading
lessons.notes_html:
The Two Steps of Editing

From the book: first revise for idea and content, then proofread for form — grammar, spelling and punctuation. In the model 'pyramids' paragraph, the last sentence about robbers is deleted as irrelevant. The edited paragraph reads: "Egyptian peasants built the pyramids. They faced a hard job. First, they had to cut the stones with saws. Then they had to drag the heavy blocks to the pyramids and shove them in place. Each block weighed more than 2 tons. They also had to push the blocks up brick ramps to get them to the top of the pyramid. As they worked higher and higher, they had to build longer ramps and pull them up."

The Corrected 'Wajid' Paragraph

"This is about Wajid. He is a new student in my English class. There are many classes at the English language centre. He generally enjoys life in the city. He has a good opinion of the university. He does not like his dormitory, though. He is 18 years old. He is from a small town in the north. He is studying business administration, English and accounting. In his free time, he plays football."

Corrections Made in the Wajid Paragraph

  • 'students' → 'student' (one new student). 'in my English' → 'in my English class'.
  • 'There many classes' → 'There are many classes' (missing verb added).
  • Small 'he' after full stops capitalised; 'english language centre' → 'English language centre'.
  • 'He studying' → 'He is studying'. 'In this free time' → 'In his free time'.

Key Points

  • Revise content first (delete irrelevant sentences), then proofread form.
  • Common errors to hunt: missing verbs, wrong possessives, small letters after full stops.

options: First revise for idea and content, then proofread for form

lessons.title: Reading: Role of the Media
lessons.notes_html:
The Fourth Pillar of Democracy

Media is known as the fourth pillar of democracy. It plays an important role in shaping public opinion and is considered the mirror of modern society — something that reflects society as it is. Newspapers (print media) are the best way of educating people politically and socially: the public read about current events, interpret them and learn to participate intelligently in the political, social and economic affairs of the country.

Forms of Media

Electronic media has emerged as a very popular form of media — a popular means of social interaction and propagation along with print media. It began with the invention of the radio, spread through television, laptops and computers via the internet, and now it is in every hand in the form of mobile phones. Social media (Facebook, YouTube, Twitter, Instagram) is also very popular these days. In the present ultramodern world, electronic media — especially the internet and social media on mobile phones — is the most widely used form of media, because it gives instant information and knowledge.

How Media Is Used

Governments and politicians utilize social media to engage with constituents (voters) and reach out to the public, sharing their policies and messages. People also use social media for career opportunities and for sharing their thoughts, feelings, insights and emotions. Media influences our daily life in every way: we update ourselves through the morning newspaper and news channels, get information, education and entertainment, and businesses reach customers through advertisements.

The Dark Side of Media

The dark side of media is that sometimes media houses lower the moral tone and publish substandard material to increase their readership and ratings. At times, newspapers ally themselves to a particular ideology or party instead of maintaining their impartiality (not taking sides), and indulge in mudslinging, defamation (damaging someone's reputation with false statements) and communal propaganda (one-sided ideas used to gain support) for easy money — which proves disastrous for society. Irresponsible media can also have a bad influence on children and teenagers.

What Media Should Aim For

Media should be aimed at human improvement. It should be used carefully and wisely: respect the privacy of others, avoid sharing harmful personal information, maintain impartiality, and look closely at what is aired. Used rightly, media may bring about a great revolution (a great change) in every field of life.

Word Meanings

  • communication: exchange of information, thoughts and feelings. interaction: conversation or exchange between people.
  • broadcaster: a person whose job is presenting on television or radio. propagation: the act of spreading ideas, beliefs or information.
  • momentum: the ability to keep increasing or developing. interpret: to explain the meaning of something. ultra: extremely; beyond.
  • impartiality: the quality of not taking sides; fairness. communal: relating to a community or religious groups.

Punctuation Practice (the Waseem paragraph)

"Waseem is one of the laziest boys I know. He is tall and slim, with black hair, and he always wears a T-shirt and black jeans. His jeans have holes in them and his cricket books are scruffy too. He usually sits at the back of the class and he often seems to be asleep. However, when the exam results are given out, he always gets 'A's. I don't think he is as lazy as he appears to be."

Key Points

  • Media = fourth pillar of democracy and mirror of society.
  • Newspapers best educate people politically and socially; electronic media is most widely used.
  • Media's aim should be human improvement, with impartiality.

lessons.title: Grammar: Plurals of Compound Nouns, Correct Spellings and Pronouns
lessons.notes_html:
Plurals of Compound Nouns

Most compound nouns take '-s' at the end; nouns ending in a sibilant sound take '-es'; and '-y' after a consonant changes to '-ies':

  • toothbrush — toothbrushes. headmaster — headmasters. armchair — armchairs.
  • butterfly — butterflies. crybaby — crybabies. footprint — footprints.
  • earring — earrings. workshop — workshops. eggplant — eggplants. blackboard — blackboards.

Correct Spellings

notebook (not 'notbook'); government (not 'goverment'); chocolate (not 'choclate'); actor (not 'acter'); stopping (not 'stoping' — double the p); finally (not 'finaly'); pattern (not 'pattren'); puzzle (not 'puzzel'); interesting (not 'intresting'); happily (not 'happyly' — y changes to i).

Pronouns — The Book's Answers

  • He is in my house.
  • To whom are you giving this gift? (whom after a preposition, as object)
  • Which of these would you like to buy? (which for a choice among known things)
  • He liked everything I bought for him.
  • Tahir and Mona are talking to each other. (two people, one to the other)
  • Who is knocking at the door? (who as subject)
  • These books are mine. (possessive pronoun standing alone)
  • I saw someone at the bus stop but I don't know who he was. (someone for a person)

Key Points

  • Who = subject; whom = object, especially after prepositions (to whom).
  • 'My' needs a noun after it; 'mine' stands alone: These books are mine.

lessons.title: Writing: Objective Summary and Dialogue Writing
lessons.notes_html:
The Objective Summary

An objective summary contains only the key ideas of the text, no personal opinion, and is shorter than the original. The book's task on the passage about electric trolley cars asks for (1) the title, (2) the main idea, and (3) the summary in our own words.

  • Title: 'The Decline of the Electric Trolley Cars in America'.
  • Main idea: The clean and comfortable electric trolley (tram) system of the United States was deliberately dismantled, most probably by powerful men of the automobile industry who worked together to replace trolleys with cars and buses.
  • Summary: Electric trolley cars were once the chief mode of public transportation in the United States. In 1922, General Motors created a special unit to replace electric trolleys with cars, trucks and buses, and over the next decade it lobbied for laws that made operating trams more difficult and less profitable. In 1936, General Motors created front companies, funded by Firestone Tire, Standard Oil of California, Phillips Petroleum and others, to purchase and dismantle the trolley car system. Although labour strikes, the Great Depression and unfavourable regulations also played a part, the primary cause was perhaps this joint effort of the auto industry to increase automobile sales.

A Model Dialogue: Salesman and Customer

The book's model dialogue is about buying a car at City Motors. The new model is comfortable, fuel-efficient and has strong safety features; it costs twenty-five lakh rupees, with a five-year warranty and free service for the first year. The customer takes a test drive, likes the car, asks for a small discount, and books it the same day.

Key Points

  • Objective = facts only, no 'I think'; a summary is shorter than the original.
  • A sales dialogue moves: greeting → needs → features → price/warranty → test drive → decision.

lessons.title: Reading Review: The Boy, Cultures Compared and Media's Role
lessons.notes_html:
The Young Boy's Adventure — Review Answers

  • The young boy (Bud) wants to go up in the plane and fly; when he saw a silver plane flying overhead, he felt that flying would be the greatest thing that could ever happen.
  • His most exciting experience was his first flight in an old open-cockpit biplane with his father at the age of eight: the plane bounced down the grass strip and rose; it banked and he could look straight down; he felt elated and could not forget the view of the sky and the feeling of being suspended without falling; everything on the ground looked as small as a toy train set.

Sindhi and Balochi Cultures Compared

  • Region and land: Sindh lies in the south along the River Indus, with fertile plains; Balochistan is an area of barren lands, deserts and mountains.
  • Language and literature: Sindhi is an ancient language rich in folklore and poetry; its greatest poet is Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai (Risalo). The Baloch speak Balochi and are famous for their storytelling tradition, in which poets and storytellers are highly respected.
  • Dress: Baloch men wear a turban with a wide loose shalwar and knee-long shirts; women's dresses have a big pocket with embroidery and round mirror work. Sindhi dress is the shalwar kameez with the traditional Sindhi cap and ajrak.
  • Food: the most well-known Baloch dish is Sajji, with wheat, millet, rice and meat; Sindhi dishes are Pallo Machi (fish), Palli, Bhee and phulka with rice.
  • Festivals and crafts: Balochistan is known for Balochi embroidery and the Sibi festival; Sindh's lifestyle is mainly agricultural with inland fishing on the Indus.

What Should Media's Role Be?

Media's role should be positive and responsible: as the fourth pillar of democracy and the mirror of society, it should shape public opinion honestly, educate people politically and socially, maintain impartiality, respect the privacy of others, avoid substandard material, mudslinging and propaganda, and aim at human improvement.

More Word Meanings

  • components: the parts of which something is made. fanatical: extremely (and unreasonably) enthusiastic about a belief or cause.
  • encompass: to include all or a large number of things. inspired: influenced or filled with a feeling or idea. deeds: actions; things done.

Oral Communication — Social Media

In the review's role-play, Azmat thinks social media kills valuable time and that false information can mislead people, while Nusrat explains the benefits — public profiles, uploading pictures and multimedia, privacy protection — and both agree that we can use social networks carefully and sensibly.

Key Points

  • Sindh: Indus plains, ajrak and cap, Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai. Balochistan: mountains and deserts, Sajji, Sibi festival.
  • Media's role: honest, impartial, aimed at human improvement.

lessons.title: Grammar Review: Compound Plurals, Future Perfect and Modals
lessons.notes_html:
Plurals of Compound Nouns — Review Answers

footballs; blackboards; toolboxes (words ending in -x take '-es'); grass-fields; sunflowers; datasets; cockpits; breakthroughs.

Future Perfect — Review Answers

  • We shall have started our journey before the day dawns. (start)
  • The bank will have opened by the time we reach there. (open)
  • The farmers will have ploughed their fields before the sun sets. (plough)
  • I shall have undertaken exercise before the sun rises. (undertake)
  • The train will have left when you arrive. (leave)
  • They will have received an award for the best performance. (receive)

Modal Auxiliaries — Review Answers

  • When she was five, she could read and write. (past ability)
  • Pick up these flowers, otherwise your mother will get angry with you.
  • We need not buy tickets. My brother has already bought them.
  • You must help your mother with the housework. She is tired.
  • I was so high up that I did not dare look down.
  • We ought to obey our elders.

Abbreviations and Acronyms — Review Answers

adj. = adjective (adjectival). Dec. = December. CAP = Community Access Point. NASA = National Aeronautics and Space Administration. National Accountability Bureau = NAB. Central Excise Duty = CED. American Dental Association = ADA. Pak-Arab Oil Refinery Company = PARCO.

Key Points

  • Future perfect = will/shall have + past participle, often with 'before' or 'by the time'.
  • could = past ability; dare = courage; ought to = moral duty.

lessons.title: Writing Review: Dialogue and Summary Writing
lessons.notes_html:
A Model Dialogue: Buying a Mobile Phone

At Mobile City, the salesman shows the latest model with a big screen, a powerful battery and an excellent camera. Its price is forty-five thousand rupees with a one-year warranty. If the customer buys today, he gets a free cover and protector glass — and he happily asks the salesman to pack the phone.

Summary of the Paragraph about Exercise

Exercise is extremely important in our daily lives because our bodies have evolved from active, nomadic ancestors and are designed to be regularly active. Sitting all day at a desk or in front of a TV can cause health problems. Exercise — bodily movement performed to develop or maintain physical fitness — reduces the risk of death, and active people increase their life expectancy by two years compared to inactive people. Regular exercise and good physical fitness improve the quality of life in many ways and help us to look good, feel good and enjoy life.

Key Points

  • A summary keeps only the main ideas of the paragraph, in our own words.
  • Key facts of the exercise paragraph: bodies are designed to be active; exercise reduces the risk of death; active people live about two years longer.
